name: Question 14
problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0<t<2\pi .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ on the curve. Determine the coordinates of the point at which the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis. Do not round the answers.

The normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}},
{{field-2}}$).$
worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=3\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point $(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6},$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,\frac{\pi }{6}} & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m:$

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{3}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=\sqrt{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-\frac{1}{2} & =\sqrt{3}(x-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\ y-\frac{1}{2} & =\sqrt{3}x-\frac{3(3)}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt{3}x-\frac{9}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt{3}x-4.\end{aligned}
$$

The normal crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at  $(0,\,-4).$

EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point C by substituting t=π6 into the parametric equations: x=3cos⁡(π6)=3⋅32=332y=sin⁡(π6)=12

So, we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point (332,12). For this, we need to find dydx, which means we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows: x′(t)=−3sin⁡t,y′(t)=cos⁡t

So, we have dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=cos⁡t−3sin⁡t=−13cot⁡t.

At the point where t=π6, the slope of the tangent line is given by m=dydx|t=π6=−13cot⁡(π6)=−13(3)=−33.

To find the slope mn of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of m: mn=−1m=−1(−33)=33=3

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point (x1,y1)=(332,12) and the slope mn=3. We get y−12=3(x−332)y−12=3x−3(3)2y=3x−92+12y=3x−4.

The normal crosses the y-axis when x=0. At this point, we have y=−4.

Consequently, the normal to the curve at C crosses the y-axis at (0,−4).
